rows.what: The Army Lists ARE walkable after all — British Army Lists & Commission Registers 1661-1826
rows.note:
**This corrects item 42, closed yesterday.** That item checked 120 Internet Archive identifiers one metadata record at a time, found exactly one volume between 1776 and 1815, and concluded «there is no digitised annual run to walk». **There is one — indexed rather than page-image, and behind this subscription.** Robert D'Arcy is in it at 1778, 1802 and 1803; in **British Army Officer Promotions 1800-1815** at 1802, 1804, 1805 and 1813; and in **Britain, Royal and Imperial Calendars 1767-1973** at 1805 and 1808. Each entry needs opening: a commission register can carry a rank, a station and sometimes a predecessor, and the Royal Calendar lists office-holders by appointment.

**Done 20 September** — written up at **/the-corps/**. Three Robert entries giving rank at both ends of the gap, George of the 39th in 1826, and a warning: **the set's `yearofrecord` filter is silently ignored**, so the 1784-1802 silence may be the publisher's and not the man's. That distinction is left open rather than resolved.

rows.what: Two D'Arcy records at the edge of the family, noted and not claimed
rows.note:
A **D'Arcy marriage at CHATHAM ST MARY in 1806**, forenames not given in the index — the parish where Robert was buried in 1827 and where Constantine was commissioned. And a **Robert D'Arcy baptised 1770 at St George, Hanover Square** — almost certainly a different man, since this archive's Robert was buried aged 76 in 1827. Both are written down because they will be found again by the next person, and **neither is claimed**.

**Done 20 September, and half of it dissolved.** The «D'Arcy marriage at Chatham St Mary in 1806» is **Margaret Maria Isabella D'Arcy to John Maddock** — this family's own marriage, already held in full, appearing in a second index under a shorter form of the groom's name. Not a record at the edge of the family at all.

The 1770 Robert could not be re-found, and that is the index's fault: D'ARCY returns nothing in England Births & Baptisms, DARCY returns entries whose **baptism-year column is empty because they are indexed by birth year**, and neither filter reaches 1770. Recorded as blocked with the controls named.

rows.what: Read all 158 Saniger baptisms with their fathers named
rows.note:
The single most productive thing the subscription has opened. **England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975** indexes a **father's first name** for every entry — 158 for this surname, 1625 to the 1820s, across Berkeley, Thornbury, Dursley, Stone and King's Stanley. One page of twenty has been read and it gave **Ann Saniger, Berkeley 1798, father John**. Eight pages in all. Read in baptism-year order it would give the whole sibling group around 1795–1815 **with their father named from record rather than from a tree** — which is the deepest line in this archive and the one that has rested on other people's trees since the beginning.

**Done 16 September.** All eight pages read. The pagination parameter is `_page`, and the columns sort with `o=fatherfirstname`, which is the single most useful thing this dataset offers. Yield: the complete Berkeley sibling group with **John named as father in the index**, a read null for Hannah under this spelling, 33 duplicate entries out of 158, and a third independent disproof of own error 32 — no Awre, no Blakeney, nothing west of the Severn in 268 years of this surname's baptisms.

rows.what: Hannah under SINEGAR and SYNEGAR
rows.note:
Of the three spellings that dominate the Berkeley registers — **SINNEGAR (92 entries), SANIGAR (74), SINEGAR (60)** — only SINNEGAR has been tried on the baptism set, with no result, and SANIGAR gave two Bristol entries of 1831. **SINEGAR and SYNEGAR have not been tried at all.** This archive's own correction 28 was caused by exactly this: a null published as «not found» when it meant «not found under the ten spellings I thought of».

**Done 16 September, and widened.** Fifteen spellings were put to the set rather than two. SINEGAR returns 28 and SYNEGAR none; ten other forms were tried beside them, and 340 entries were read in all. Written up at **/spellings**, which is now the page any future null about this surname has to be graded against.

rows.what: The 1804 «Jno Saniger» at Berkeley with no father indexed
rows.note:
The complete pass turned up one entry it cannot place: **Jno Saniger, Berkeley, 1804, father column empty** — the only Berkeley Saniger baptism in the whole 158 with no father named. Hannah Sanigor was baptised at Berkeley on 18 August 1804 and her brother Jno on 18 September 1803. Three readings: a second son born the same year as Hannah, a mis-indexed second copy of the 1803 entry, or a different family. **The register page for 1804 settles it in one look** and the archive has not looked.

**Settled 20 September, and it was none of the three readings.** The transcripts show the 1803 entry naming **a father and no mother** and the 1804 entry naming **a mother, MARY SANIGER, and no father** — five months apart at consecutive index numbers. A named mother beside an empty father's column is a **base-born child**, and Hannah's mother was Lydia. Not this family.

rows.what: Put the fifteen spellings to the marriage and burial sets as well
rows.note:
The spelling sweep was run on baptisms only. **England Marriages 1538-1973** and **England Deaths & Burials 1538-1991** take the same query, the same fifteen strings and the same `_page` pagination, and the baptism sweep has just shown what that method is worth: it found the 1632-1676 Berkeley «gap» was a spelling. Marriages would also test the FamilySearch tree's unsourced claim that **John Saniger married Lydia Jones at Berkeley in 1797**, which is the oldest open question on this archive's direct line.

**Done 16 September for marriages.** Eight spellings, 135 entries. It settled the Lydia Jones question in an afternoon: the tree's marriage is John **Sawyer**, not John Saniger, and Lydia's death is confirmed in the GRO index. **Burials are still not done** — see the row below.

rows.what: The Cotswold-scarp family — Abraham of Dursley and Daniel of Cam
rows.note:
The sweep turned up a whole second family this archive has never written about: the **-INEG- spellings** cluster at **Dursley, Cam, Stinchcombe, North Nibley and Alderley** from 1648, with two clear patriarchs — **Abraham at Dursley**, children 1698-1720, and **Daniel at Cam**, children 1729-1760, eight of them. This archive's own Hannah lived as SINEGAR in Bristol. Whether the Vale and the scarp are one family or two is **not answered** by a baptism index, and the honest next step is the Dursley and Cam registers themselves, not more index work.

**Done 20 September** — written up at **/spellings/** as «The other family, on the scarp»: six patriarchs, their children, the two repeated forenames that imply unlooked-for burials, and an explicit refusal to join them to the Vale on the strength of a baptism index.

rows.what: The burial set, under all fifteen spellings
rows.note:
Baptisms and marriages have both been swept. **England Deaths & Burials 1538-1991** has not been, and it is the set that would give **John Saniger's burial at Berkeley in January 1825** from an index rather than from the tree this archive already corrected once, and would test whether Lydia was buried at Berkeley beside him after her death was registered at Thornbury in 1851.

**Done 16 September, and it is a dead end by measurement.** The set holds 23 SANIGER burials, all Berkeley, none after **1787**. Controlled by asking for every Berkeley burial of any surname: **442 in 1735-1765, two in 1800-1830**. The index stops. That closes the route rather than answering the question, and it is now a coverage row so no future session spends a morning on it.

rows.what: Lydia's maiden name, from a source that is not a tree
rows.note:
JONES is now **disputed**, not «a name to test». Three places could still give it honestly: the **Berkeley marriage register itself** for 1795-1798, which the index may simply not transcribe; **Hannah's or her siblings' marriage entries after 1837**, which name fathers but not mothers, so no; or the **1851 census**, if Lydia was still alive in March and living with a relative whose relationship to her is stated. She died in the third quarter of that year, so **the 1851 census should have caught her** — and it has not been searched for her.

**16 September, partly answered.** The 1851 census found her: Ham, Berkeley, 81, born «Wooton under Edge», mother-in-law to her widowed daughter-in-law. That confirms the birthplace and the year. It does **not** give a maiden name — the census never does — so JONES stands disputed and the Berkeley marriage register itself is now the only honest route left.

**20 September: narrowed hard, and still open.** Three tests, all null and all controlled — the Ham neighbours; her own parish of Wotton-under-Edge, where the single candidate turned out to have married a **Cossens**; and **every spelling across the whole country, 1790-1802, which returns nothing at all**. Berkeley and Wotton are both well covered, so the marriage is in neither. What is left is the **register itself** or the **diocesan licence bonds**.

**21 September: the index route is exhausted, and one of the four readings is closed.** The surname box takes wildcards, so the question was asked with **no spelling assumed at all**. `S*N*G*` across Gloucestershire marriages for 1793-1803 returns **122 rows, all read**: six are really this surname and **not one is a John, and not one marries a Lydia**. A John of any `S*N*G*` surname marrying a Lydia **anywhere in England** between 1780 and 1820 returns sixteen, and the only arguable one is a Wiltshire SANGER at Salisbury in 1788. **The reading that the entry was hiding under an untried spelling can be retired** — and the sweep proved itself by turning up SINIGOR and SINNIGER, two forms missing from the spelling table rebuilt that morning. What remains needs **the Berkeley register itself**, which is the blocked letter to Gloucestershire Archives.

rows.what: Read the spouse's surname, always
rows.note:
A method note that cost the wider internet twenty years. FindMyPast's marriage result rows show first name, spouse's **first** name, year, place and county — and **not the spouse's surname**, which is one click away on the transcript. Every marriage this archive has ever cited from a result row rather than a transcript should be re-opened. **This is a worklist item, not a finding, until that audit is done.**

**Done 17 September. 51 marriage entries audited; 5 were at risk; 4 re-opened and confirmed; 1 named as unchecked.** Nothing was wrong. The audit is still worth its morning, because «nothing was wrong» is a result and «we never looked» is not — and it established that the missing spouse surname is FindMyPast's result-row design across collections, not one dataset's quirk. Written up at **/behind-the-paywall/**.

rows.what: Order the death certificate of John Sanigar, Thornbury, Q1 1850
rows.note:
The one document that would turn an inference into a fact. Ann Sanigar is a widow at Ham in 1851 with children baptised to a father John; a John Sanigar's death is registered in that district in the first quarter of 1850; and Hannah's brother John, baptised Berkeley 18 September 1803, would have been 46. **The certificate gives age at death and occupation**, and the 1851 census already says the husband was a **tailor**. If it says 46 and tailor, the identification is closed. It costs the GRO's standard fee.

**20 September: reclassified as blocked on David — it needs a GRO fee, which this archive cannot supply.**

rows.what: Work the whole Ham and Clapton neighbourhood, not just the surname
rows.note:
Both censuses give a **street and a schedule number**, which means the neighbours can be read off the same pages — HO107/347 bk 6 f.3 p.1 for 1841 and HO107/1957 f.561 p.13 for 1851. A surname search finds a family; **an address search finds who they married**. Lydia's maiden name is much more likely to be a name on the same two pages than a name in an index.

**Done 20 September, and it did not answer the question.** The neighbours are read by walking the household transcript identifiers, which run in sequence along the enumerator's round — a method worth keeping. Samuel Nelmes one side, Stephen Smith the farmer the other; no relative of Lydia's, no Jones in the village.

rows.what: The Mazza fault, checked for here and found
rows.note: The estate landing page caught Mazza building per-person data without reading either of its two evidence files. **This archive had the same fault in a different shape.** Every data file here has a reader, so the coarse check passed — but `build_dossiers.py` drops every register record row whose name the family tree also carries, and `/people/[slug]` never read them. **176 record lines, 55 people, 30 of them with pages saying no record had been found.** Fixed with `tools/build_person_records.py`, a records section on the person page, an honest sentence in `grade.js`, and a gate in `check_links.py` that reads register.json rather than its own output. Control-tested three ways, all exit 1.

rows.what: Settle the eight shared names, or say why they cannot be settled
rows.note:
The join from a record to a person is a **name**, because register record rows carry no id. Forty-seven names match one person. **Eight match between two and four**: William Sneyd (4), Thomas Saniger, Catherine D'Arcy, Constantine D'Arcy, George Pitt D'Arcy, James Sneyd, Mary Sneyd, Samuel Charles Sneyd. Their records are shown on every candidate's page under «filed under the name, not assigned to this person», which is honest but is not an answer. **Most are separable on a date** — Thomas Saniger's eight lines run 1711 to 1881 and plainly belong to at least three men. The `rec()` calls in build_register.py could take an optional slug, the way `ids_for()` already takes a «Name|1810» hint.

**Done 20 September. Seven settled, one refused, and one surprise.** The rules live in `tools/record-owners.json`, each naming a distinguishing string from a record's own text and the slug it belongs to, and the build refuses a rule that never fires — which immediately caught two redundant ones.

**WILLIAM SNEYD is left unsettled on purpose.** Four men of the name, and the records contradict each other: the weaver who married Mary Blackbourne in 1769 has a baptism of 1742 in the record and a birth of 1746 in the tree, and two burials give births of about 1731 and about 1743, so at most one can be his. Choosing would be inventing a man.

**The surprise: THOMAS SANIGER is three men, not two.** Four of his eight records belong to a Thomas baptised at Berkeley on 3 July 1808, son of John, Hannah's brother — **who is not in the family tree at all**. Showing them on both tree Thomases had been offering a reader two men born ninety-seven years apart as candidates for a life that belonged to neither. They now appear on no person page, which is correct; he is written about at **/thomas-sinegar/**, and both tree Thomases link to him.

rows.what: Audit the other five silent joins the same way
rows.note:
The fault was a build script assuming a page would show something it never read. The same shape is possible in five other places, and none has been control-tested: **mentions.json** (matches name phrases in rendered HTML — 13 of the 55 got zero), the hand-kept **APPEARS_IN**, **VERIFIED** and **PORTRAITS** maps inside `/people/[slug].astro`, and **graves.json** and **households.json**, which both key people by slug and are read only by their own pages. **Ask of each: if this map went empty, would anything refuse?**

**Done 20 September. One real loss found, and it was not the one expected.** No second instance of the record-row fault: `graves.json` and `households.json` do not reach the person page directly, but the facts they carry — the burial place, the marriage, the children — are already on the page from the family tree, so nothing is dropped. All 101 burial places check out.

**What was dropped was in a hand-kept map.** `APPEARS_IN` carried `hannah-saniger` twice, four links then two, and in a JavaScript object literal the second silently wins. **The direct line of this archive had lost her voyage on the General Hewitt.** Fixed, and `check_links.py` now refuses a duplicate key, a key naming a person with no page, and a grave whose place the person's own page does not state. Control-tested three ways.

rows.what: Whether to pay the RCB Library's search fee for the Wicklow marriage

The RCB Library replied on 16 September and **offered to search their registers on request, fee quoted on application**. Their registers are not online and never have been, so this is the only route left to the marriage of **George Pitt D'Arcy and Maria White, Co. Wicklow, about 1819**. Two things are needed before asking: **a parish, or a short list of them**, because a county-wide manual search is not a reasonable thing to ask for, and **a decision on the money**, which is not this archive's to make.

**17 September: the blocker is cleared.** The parishes can now be named. **Bray (1670-1956), Wicklow town (1729-1998) and Arklow (1798-1861)** are the three to ask for first.

rows.what: Read the Wicklow holdings list from somewhere that is not churchofireland.org
rows.note:

**Done 17 September, in an ordinary browser.** The Cloudflare interstitial cleared by itself — a different client, nothing solved. 25 parishes named, with their marriage date ranges, on **/george-pitt/**. The three garrison parishes — **Bray, Wicklow town, Arklow** — all have registers covering 1819, which is what the RCB Library needs before a paid search is worth buying.

rows.note:

Checked now rather than argued.

rows.what: Order or read the ten non-Berkeley medieval documents
rows.note:
The API gives references, not documents. **C 241/174/26 and C 131/202/27** (the £400 staple debt of 1385) are at Kew; **MS 3549/4, /20 and /187** are at Birmingham Archives in the Fletcher collection, which is where John Smyth's own papers ended up; **DE/M/95** is at Hertfordshire Archives; **E 40/12147** at Kew; **P/St.P and J/D/2(j)** at Bristol Archives. rows.what: Re-run every old Discovery null through the API
rows.note:
Two nulls fell on 17 September the moment the same question was asked through the API instead of the search box — the partition of 1347, and Peddington. **There are 37 Discovery rows in searched.json and several are nulls.** Each one should be put through `tools/discovery.py` before it is trusted, because a null typed into a box is a null about the box.

**Done 17 September. Six re-run: one overturned, three confirmed, two not testable by query.** The overturned one is the important one and the lesson is narrower than «the API is better»: the 1346 partition was missed because the old search asked for «de Wyke» beside two other words rather than for the phrase **«John de Wyke»**. The catalogue was fine. **A null carries the shape of the question that produced it**, and that is now true of a search box and an API equally.

rows.what: Edward Sanniger, mariner of Chepstow, 1806
rows.note:
Two records for one man, found in the surname sweep and never seen here before: **IR 26/352/152**, the Death Duty abstract of his will, proved November 1806, at Kew; and **LL/1806/24** at the **National Library of Wales**, the Llandaff probate itself. **Chepstow is directly across the Severn from Berkeley**, and a mariner is exactly how a Vale surname crosses water. Not claimed as kin — there is nothing joining him to this family yet.

**Done 20 September.** Both references confirmed — IR 26/352/152 at Kew (the Death Duty abstract) and LL/1806/24 at the National Library of Wales (the will itself). Recorded as a lead, not a relative: nothing joins him to this family.

rows.what: The two Discovery nulls that a query cannot re-test
rows.note:
«232 Wakefield-and-Bristol hits and not one is this family» and «no D'Arcy will for Kent between 1820 and 1860» are **readings, not queries**, so re-running them proves nothing. They can only be re-tested by reading the 232, which `tools/discovery.py` can now dump to a file in one call. Until someone does, they are the weakest nulls on the site — and they are about **three of the four British lines**.

**Partly done 20 September.** A hundred of the 232 Wakefield-and-Bristol records read by machine against every forename in the household: three name-matches, all Chancery causes of 1869, fifteen years after the family sailed. **132 remain unread** — and fixing `discovery.py`'s pagination is what makes finishing them possible.

rows.note:
Liz at Trove Support (RSref189042) would not issue a key until four things were answered: what tools will use the data **and their names**; **whether the tool has AI components and how Trove data would be used with AI**; whether it will be shared and freely; and why the API is needed rather than the website.

rows.what: Gloucester diocesan marriage licence bonds and allegations, 1795-1799
rows.note:
The marriage of **John Saniger and Lydia** is not in England Marriages 1538-1973 under any of eight spellings anywhere in England between 1790 and 1802, against two well-covered candidate parishes. If they married **by licence** the register entry may be brief or the parish unexpected, but the **allegation and bond survive separately at Gloucestershire Archives (GDR)** and name both parties, their parishes, their ages or condition, and frequently the bride's father. **That is the document that would give her maiden name.** This archive already has one GDR errand open (GDR/B4/1/387) and could ask for both together.

**20 September: reclassified as blocked on David — it needs the Gloucestershire Archives letter, which this archive cannot supply.**

rows.what: Letter to Gloucestershire Archives — four references, drafted and unsent
rows.note:
Drafted 20 September at `notes/letters/2026-09-20-gloucestershire-archives.md`. **It asks for nothing they have already refused.** Andrew Parry said on 14 September that they offer no research service, so this asks only the three things such a repository will still do: what a finding aid covers, what a reference physically consists of, and a quote to copy a document named by reference.

Four asks, in order: **(1)** whether the Gloucester diocesan **marriage allegations and bonds** of the 1790s are name-indexed — the only route left to Lydia's maiden name; **(2)** a copy quote for **GDR/B4/1/387**; **(3)** a copy quote for **D5555/2/9**, the 1608 muster and hearth tax transcripts; **(4)** whether an item-level list exists for **D2957/41**. It closes by asking for their **list of independent researchers**, which is the most valuable ask if the rest disappoints. **David to review, amend and send.**

rows.what: The 237 people with an empty mentions list
rows.note:
`mentions.json` holds 459 keys and **only 222 are non-empty** — half the published people are written about nowhere on this site. That is not a bug: `build_mentions.py` deliberately skips the directory pages (`/people`, `/register`, `/graves`, `/households`, `/families`, `/who`, `/places`, `/marriages`, `/search`) because «a name in a card grid is not a mention», which is right. But it means **the mention count is a measure of prose, not of evidence**, and this archive should not let the two be confused on a page that shows both.

**Done 20 September.** The distribution: **237 of 473 people have no mention at all, 142 have exactly one, and 80 have two or more.** That is not a bug — `build_mentions.py` skips the directory pages on purpose — but the person page was calling the result «the same evidence as the rest of the archive», which is two claims too many. **Fourteen of the 237 with no mention have a register record.** The sentence now says a mention counts pages of prose, not records, and that a person can be well documented and appear there once or not at all.

rows.what: Give Thomas Saniger of 1808 a page, or say why he has none
rows.note:
The settling of the shared names turned up a man with **four records and no page**: Thomas Saniger, baptised Berkeley 3 July 1808, son of John, Hannah's brother — married Martha Golding at Bristol in 1828, living at Sion Road in 1841, died at Waterloo Lane in 1881 and buried at Greenbank. He is not in the family tree, so `/people/` has nothing for him, and `build_dossiers.py` skips him because the tree carries his NAME. **He falls between both mechanisms.** /thomas-sinegar/ writes about him, which is why this is a tidying job and not a loss.

**Done 20 September.** `build_dossiers.py` now reads `tools/record-owners.json` and gives a page to records the rules assign to **nobody in the tree**. Thomas Saniger of 1808 has one at **/who/thomas-saniger/**, carrying his four records and saying plainly that the tree holds his name and not him, with a pointer to **/thomas-sinegar/** where he is written about under the spelling Bristol gave him. The mechanism is general: any future record settled onto nobody gets a page instead of vanishing.

rows.what: Audit that everything researched has actually reached the site
rows.note:
`tools/check_published.py`, wired into the build. It refuses a data file no page imports, and a signpost whose `href` is not a built page; it warns where a page carries nothing distinctive from the row pointing at it.

**First run: 55 data files, 498 signposts, 0 orphans, 0 dangling — and two real faults.** Three searched rows pointed at **/what-we-got-wrong**, which is a redirect stub, so a reader landed on a redirect instead of /corrections/. And **the whole body of tax-record research had no home**: E 179's six Tudor subsidy pieces for Berkeley hundred, the hearth tax at Kew and Gloucester, the bundle D5555/2/9 transcribing three sources at once, and the documented absence of Berkeley from the 1381 poll tax — all researched in September, all signposted to **/swonhungre/**, and that page never mentioned a tax. Now written up there as «The tax records, which are the bridge»: they are what crosses the century and a half between the last medieval deed and the first readable register.

rows.what: Four spelling clusters read, two refused, and the fold map wired to something
rows.note:
`namefold.py --root site --all` offered four folds and waited, correctly, for the archive that owns the names.

**FOLDED: SANYGER → Saniger** (22 tokens). It is one of the four spellings Maclean's edition of the 1608 muster gives for this family — Saniger 5, Sanyger 3, Syniger 2, Sainger 1. The same name.

**REFUSED: ZANIGAR → Sanigar.** ZANIGAR is not a spelling of anything. **This archive invented it on 17 September as a nonsense control** to test whether Discovery's search was loosely fuzzy, and its null is why the counts on /spellings/ can be trusted. Folding it would hand a control test to anyone searching for the family, and would make the archive appear to hold it as attested.

**REFUSED: LION → Lyon.** Every LION in this archive is the **Persian Order of the Lion and Sun**, Joseph D'Arcy's decoration from the Shah. LYON is one real person, Lydia Lyon. The fold would have meant that searching a woman's surname returned a knighthood.

Both refusals and their reasons are in **`site/src/data/namefold-deny.json`**, so the next session to run the tool does not overturn them on sight.

**And the map was reaching nobody.** It was generated and no page passed a `fold` prop — the same fault this archive spent the day hunting. It is now wired into **/register/, /searched/, /places/ and /graves/**. Not into /search/: the kit's Search component carries its own accent-folding function that must stay identical to `searchkit.py`, and site-wide variants are already handled by ALIASES in `build_search.py`.

rows.what: The living rule now covers the JSON this site serves, not only its HTML
rows.note:
A peer session pointed out that `checkliving.feed()` walks **.html** and that an atlas serves its places as JSON and a search box its index the same way. This site ships three: **searchindex.json at 2.1MB, atlas-data.json, whoindex.json** — regenerated from the tree on every build and **never opened by the gate**.

**Checked by hand first: nothing is leaking.** A substring sweep reports 25 hits and every one is noise — «George» inside George Pitt D'Arcy, «William Murdoch» inside Keith William Murdoch 1925-1996, «Geraldine» inside Geraldine D'Arcy 1872-1937.

`tools/check_living.py` now has a **json_pass** that asks the narrower and better question: not whether a living name occurs somewhere in two megabytes of text, but whether **a file names a living person AS A PERSON** — a whole-field match on `{"k":"Person","t":…}`, on `"people":[{"n":…}]`, on a whoindex triple. **917 person names across the three files; none is living.**

It makes the same **exact-namesake subtraction** feed() makes, because without it the gate fired on the published William Murdoch of 1856 and James Atwell of 1853-1907 — and in a family that reuses forenames this relentlessly, a gate that cries wolf is switched off inside a week.

**Control-tested by injecting one living person, read from the gitignored GEDCOM at run time, into the gitignored dist and never printed: clean exits 0, leaking exits 1, restored exits 0.**

rows.what: A gate against restating a reading this archive has withdrawn
rows.note:
Built from a peer session's `checkretired.py` idea, and it needed two corrections before it was worth running.

**It works because a retired phrase is this archive's own wording and never a document's.** Nobody quotes a source saying «a blank of twenty-four years»; if the string is on a page, this archive put it there.

**Two entries came straight back out on the first run.** «No record has been found for them» is not a withdrawn wording — it is a sentence false about thirty people and true about four hundred, and grade.js was fixed on 17 September to say it only when true. «May never have existed» reached ten person pages only inside **mention snippets** quoting /open-questions. A phrase belongs on this list only if it is a **proposition withdrawn in every context**.

**And quoted is not asserted.** This archive's rule is that an error stays on the page where it was made, which *guarantees* retired phrases appear in live prose — inside the sentence withdrawing them. The gate tests whether an occurrence falls inside a quoted span, not the two characters either side, which was the first version and missed a quotation nine words long. Dated logs — worklist, searched, changes, errands — are exempt outright: **they record what was believed on a day and must never be edited when the belief changes.**

It found two genuine restatements, both of «a blank of twenty-four years» in reported speech on /the-corps and /crossread. Both now quote the phrase, which is better prose as well as a passing gate. **Control-tested: asserted exits 1, the same phrase quoted exits 0.**

rows.what: Recount the spelling table on one basis, and put SANIGOR in it
rows.note:
/sanigers carries a table of **19 spellings with occurrence counts**, described as «entries in the parish registers read for this archive». **SANIGOR is not in it** — the spelling Hannah was baptised under, and the reason this archive declared her baptism missing twice. Nor is **SYNIGAR**, the four King's Stanley children of 1591-96 that are the oldest register entries the surname produces.

Both are named beside the table rather than added to it, because the sweep that found them counted against **England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975** and the table counts something else. **Putting them in the column would mix two bases quietly**, which is the fault this archive spent 21 September removing from its own prose. The fix is to recount every row on one stated basis; the counts as they stand are not wrong, they are just not comparable with the new ones.

The two cardinals in that section now derive from the table's own length.

**Done 21 September. Recounted on one stated basis and SANIGOR is in it.** England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975, searched nationally, every form put the same way: **24 spellings, 19 productive, 371 baptisms**. Nine forms from the old table had never been swept at all. **The old counts are kept in the data as `spellingsOld` rather than deleted** — they were not wrong, they were a different measure, and deleting them would hide why the numbers moved.

/spellings was brought onto the same figure, because two pages giving different totals for one thing is the fault this archive spent the previous night removing. Its dek derives from the table now, and **it is no longer called «Fifteen Spellings»** — a title that states a count goes stale the moment the count moves.

**Corrected 21 September, twice, within a day of being published.** The recount was right to insist on one basis and wrong about what that basis counts. It said **371 baptisms**; the number is **371 index entries**, and the five largest forms read row by row are **246 baptisms**. And «one basis» had quietly become «one basis decides which questions get asked»: the list of forms came from a baptism index, so **SANIGRE** — which occurs in no baptism register and carries Thomas Sinegar's marriage — was never asked. It is in the table now at nought, which is where a form that is empty in one set and decisive in another belongs.

rows.what: Find the 1852 marriage of James Sinegar, offered unasked by Bristol Archives
rows.note:
Holly Aylward at Bristol Archives ended her reply with a record nobody had asked for: «there is also a marriage certificate from 1852 for what looks like Thomas's son, James, and this record contains more information, such as Thomas's profession which is listed as **Labourer**.»

**This archive does not hold it.** James is the eleven-year-old in Thomas's house in 1841 and the father of Lydia Sinegar baptised in 1866, and there is nothing between.

It matters more than a second-generation marriage usually would, because of what the 1828 entry turned out not to carry. **A marriage of 1852 is after civil registration and names both fathers.** It cannot reach John Saniger — it names Thomas, who is the man already known — but it fixes James to this Thomas in a document, and Holly has already read the occupation off it: Labourer, which is what the 1851 census called him the year before.

Free routes first: the GRO index for a Sinegar/Sanigar marriage in the Bristol district in 1852, under every form in the table. The certificate itself is a fee, and that goes on the blocked list, not here.

**A short follow-up is drafted and not sent**, asking Holly for the reference only — parish, date and register reference — since she has already read the record and can give it in a sentence. It also asks whether the register hand is a clear SANIGAR at that word, because this archive would rather publish an ambiguity than pick a side. It asks for no further lookup.
